entries.title: Chatter: get channel
Chatter: list messages
entries.description:
GET /channels/{channel_id}/messages

Read a channel's recent messages. This is the triage read, and the only one: Chatter exposes no message search to bot applications, so finding something means paging this and filtering yourself. Newest first by default, up to `limit: 100` per call. Page *backwards* through history with `before` set to the oldest id you have seen; page forward for new arrivals with `after` set to the newest. `around` centres on one message. If every `content` comes back empty, the Message Content intent is switched off for this application — that is a toggle in the developer portal, not a permission on the invite, and nothing else reports it.

Also: chat, server, community.

entries.title: Chatter: create message
entries.description:
POST /channels/{channel_id}/messages

Post a message to a channel, as the bot application — it will carry an APP badge and the application's own name and avatar. To post under your own name instead, use `execute_webhook`. For a plain message, pass `content` (up to 2000 characters, Chatter-flavoured markdown). For an announcement, prefer `embeds`: an embed gives you a title, a coloured left border, a description, and up to 25 name/value `fields`, and it is what makes a post read as deliberate rather than typed. `color` is a decimal integer, not a hex string — 0x5865F2 is 5793266. Set `allowed_mentions` explicitly on anything that could ping a room: `{"parse": []}` suppresses every mention even if the text contains @everyone. Reply to something by passing `message_reference` with the message id. Attachments are not available here — files need a multipart request, which Chatter accepts and this connector cannot encode.

Also: chat, server, community.

entries.title: Chatter: list pins
entries.description:
GET /channels/{channel_id}/messages/pins

The pinned messages in a channel. Pinning is how this integration marks something as handled or important where a human will see it, so this is the read that shows what has been marked. Note the path is the current one — Chatter also serves a deprecated pins endpoint that is not exposed here.

Also: chat, server, message, community.

entries.title: Chatter: create pin
Chatter: get message
Chatter: update message
Chatter: delete message
Chatter: crosspost message
entries.description:
POST /channels/{channel_id}/messages/{message_id}/crosspost

Publish a message that was posted in an *announcement* channel out to every server that follows it. This is what makes an announcement channel worth using: subscribers see the post in their own server without joining yours. Only works on channel `type: 5`, and only on a message already posted there — so the sequence is `create_message` then this, with the id it returned. Rate limited far more tightly than posting, and it cannot be undone.

Also: chat, community.

entries.title: Chatter: list message reactions by emoji
Chatter: add my message reaction
entries.description:
PUT /channels/{channel_id}/messages/{message_id}/reactions/{emoji_name}/@me

React to a message as this application. The cheapest way to mark a message as seen, triaged, or categorised — a ✅ or 👀 costs nothing, notifies nobody, and is visible to everyone reading the channel. Pass a Unicode emoji directly (`emoji_name: "✅"`); a custom server emoji is `name:id`. Remove one with the matching delete tool, which is not exposed here.

Also: chat, community.

entries.title: Chatter: create thread from message
entries.description:
POST /channels/{channel_id}/messages/{message_id}/threads

Start a thread hanging off an existing message, which is how a post becomes a discussion without cluttering the channel. `name` is the thread title and is required. `auto_archive_duration` is in minutes and accepts only 60, 1440, 4320, or 10080. Use this to route a triaged message somewhere people can talk about it, rather than replying inline where it scrolls away.

Also: chat, server, community.

entries.title: Chatter: list channel webhooks
entries.description:
GET /channels/{channel_id}/webhooks

The webhooks already configured on a channel, with their ids and tokens. Check here before calling `create_webhook`: a channel accumulates a webhook per call and there is a limit of 15, so reusing the one you made last time is the difference between a working integration and a channel full of clutter. Needs Manage Webhooks. The response includes each webhook's token, which is a credential — see the note on `execute_webhook`.

Also: chat, server, message, community.

entries.title: Chatter: create webhook
entries.description:
POST /channels/{channel_id}/webhooks

Create a webhook on a channel, which is what makes posting under your own name possible. Do this once per channel and keep the id and token; call `list_channel_webhooks` first to find an existing one rather than making another. `name` is a fallback label only — the name and avatar that actually appear are the ones passed per message to `execute_webhook`. `avatar` takes a base64 data URI, not a URL, and is optional. Needs Manage Webhooks. The returned `token` is a standalone credential: anybody holding it can post to this channel without any other authentication.

Also: chat, server, community.

entries.title: Chatter: get guild
Chatter: list guild channels
entries.description:
GET /guilds/{guild_id}/channels

Every channel in a server, which is how a channel *name* becomes the `channel_id` the posting and reading tools require. Check the `type` field before posting: 0 is a normal text channel, 5 is an announcement channel (the only kind `crosspost_message` works on), 15 is a forum, and 2 and 13 are voice and stage, which cannot take messages. `parent_id` is the category a channel sits under.

Also: chat, message, community.

entries.title: Chatter: get active guild threads
entries.description:
GET /guilds/{guild_id}/threads/active

Every thread in a server that is not archived, across all channels at once. Cheaper than walking channels one at a time when the question is "what conversations are open right now", which is the usual first step of a triage pass.

Also: chat, channel, message, community.

entries.title: Chatter: get my user
entries.description:
GET /users/@me

Returns the bot application this token belongs to — its id, username, and discriminator. Costs nothing and needs no permissions, so it is the call to make first when a connection is misbehaving: a 401 here means the stored token is wrong or is missing its `Bot ` prefix, and everything else will fail the same way.

Also: chat, server, channel, message, community.

entries.title: Chatter: list my guilds
entries.description:
GET /users/@me/guilds

The servers this bot has been added to — not the servers you are a member of. A server the bot was never invited to is invisible here and unreachable by every other tool, so an empty list means the invite step was missed rather than that you have no servers. Returns id, name, and your permissions in each. Start here to turn a server name into the id every other call wants.

Also: chat, channel, message, community.

entries.title: Postbox: batch modify messages
entries.description:
Modifies the labels on the specified messages.

Postbox has no separate verb for read-state, archiving, or spam — each one is a label edit, and this is the operation that makes it: `addLabelIds: ["UNREAD"]` marks unread and `removeLabelIds: ["UNREAD"]` marks read; `removeLabelIds: ["INBOX"]` archives; `addLabelIds: ["SPAM"], removeLabelIds: ["INBOX"]` reports spam; `addLabelIds: ["STARRED"]` stars. Moving a message into a folder is the same shape — add that folder's label id and remove "INBOX" — because a Postbox folder *is* a label. Call `labels_list` for the ids of the ones the user made; the capitalised ones above are system labels and always exist. To delete mail, use the `trash` operation rather than a label: it is recoverable and there is no permanent-delete tool here by design. This is the batch form: pass up to 1000 message ids in `ids`.

Also: email, reply, correspondence.

entries.description:

entries.title: Postbox: modify messages
entries.description:
Modifies the labels on the specified message.

Postbox has no separate verb for read-state, archiving, or spam — each one is a label edit, and this is the operation that makes it: `addLabelIds: ["UNREAD"]` marks unread and `removeLabelIds: ["UNREAD"]` marks read; `removeLabelIds: ["INBOX"]` archives; `addLabelIds: ["SPAM"], removeLabelIds: ["INBOX"]` reports spam; `addLabelIds: ["STARRED"]` stars. Moving a message into a folder is the same shape — add that folder's label id and remove "INBOX" — because a Postbox folder *is* a label. Call `labels_list` for the ids of the ones the user made; the capitalised ones above are system labels and always exist. To delete mail, use the `trash` operation rather than a label: it is recoverable and there is no permanent-delete tool here by design.

entries.title: Postbox: create filters
entries.description:
Creates a filter. Note: you can only create a maximum of 1,000 filters.

This is how a sender is blocked, as opposed to reported. Reporting spam is a one-off label edit on messages that already exist — use `messages_modify` with `addLabelIds: ["SPAM"]` for that. A filter is a standing rule applied to mail that has not arrived yet: `criteria: {from: "ada.lovelace@example.com"}` with `action: {addLabelIds: ["TRASH"]}` to bin it on arrival, or `action: {addLabelIds: ["SPAM"]}` to route it to spam. `criteria` also matches on `to`, `subject`, `query`, and `hasAttachment`. The rule keeps running until it is deleted — it outlives this session, so prefer the one-off label edit unless a standing rule is what was asked for.

Also: email, message, inbox, reply, correspondence.

entries.title: Postbox: delete filters
entries.description:

entries.title: Postbox: modify threads
entries.description:
Modifies the labels applied to the thread. This applies to all messages in the thread.

Postbox has no separate verb for read-state, archiving, or spam — each one is a label edit, and this is the operation that makes it: `addLabelIds: ["UNREAD"]` marks unread and `removeLabelIds: ["UNREAD"]` marks read; `removeLabelIds: ["INBOX"]` archives; `addLabelIds: ["SPAM"], removeLabelIds: ["INBOX"]` reports spam; `addLabelIds: ["STARRED"]` stars. Moving a message into a folder is the same shape — add that folder's label id and remove "INBOX" — because a Postbox folder *is* a label. Call `labels_list` for the ids of the ones the user made; the capitalised ones above are system labels and always exist. To delete mail, use the `trash` operation rather than a label: it is recoverable and there is no permanent-delete tool here by design. This applies to every message in the thread at once.

Also: email, reply, correspondence.

The file comes back with an id the Sheets and Docs tools then work on directly — creating a spreadsheet and filling it is this call followed by `sheets_spreadsheets_values_update`. Place it by passing `parents` with a folder id.

entries.title: Filestore: update files

This is also how a file is moved, renamed, and deleted. Move it by passing `addParents` with the destination folder id and `removeParents` with the current one — a Drive file has no path, only parents. Rename it with `name`. Delete it with `trashed: true`, which is recoverable; there is deliberately no permanent-delete tool here, because Drive has a trash and an agent should not be able to bypass it. Restore with `trashed: false`.

Also: document, upload, download, attachment, storage.

entries.title: Gridwork: get spreadsheets
entries.description:
Returns the spreadsheet at the given ID. The caller must specify the spreadsheet ID. By default, data within grids is not returned. You can include grid data in one of 2 ways: * Specify a [field mask](https://example.test/docs example.test/sheets/api/guides/field-masks) listing your desired fields using the `fields` URL parameter in HTTP * Set the includeGridData URL parameter to true. If a field mask is set, the `includeGridData` parameter is ignored For large spreadsheets, as a best practice, retrieve only the specific spreadsheet fields that you want. To retrieve only subsets of spreadsheet data, use the ranges URL parameter. Ranges are specified using [A1 notation](/sheets/api/guides/concepts#cell). You can define a single cell (for example, `A1`) or multiple cells (for example, `A1:D5`). You can also get cells from other sheets within the same spreadsheet (for example, `Sheet2!A1:C4`) or retrieve multiple ranges at once (for example, `?ranges=A1:D5&ranges=Sheet2!A1:C4`). Limiting the range returns only the portions of the spreadsheet that intersect the requested ranges.

Reads an existing spreadsheet. To create one, use `drive_files_create` with `mimeType: "application/vnd.Gridwork-apps.spreadsheet"`, then write into it with the `values_*` tools — this provider edits spreadsheets but does not create the file.

Also: table, csv, row, column, formula.

entries.title: Gridwork: copy to sheets
entries.description:
Copies a single sheet from a spreadsheet to another spreadsheet. Returns the properties of the newly created sheet.

Copies one tab into a *different* spreadsheet. To duplicate a tab within the same file use `batchUpdate` with a `duplicateSheet` request, and to copy the whole file use `drive_files_copy`.

Also: table, csv, row, column, formula.

entries.title: Gridwork: get values
entries.description:
Returns a range of values from a spreadsheet. The caller must specify the spreadsheet ID and a range.

Also: table, csv, row, column, formula.

entries.title: Gridwork: update values
entries.description:
Sets values in a range of a spreadsheet. The caller must specify the spreadsheet ID, range, and a valueInputOption.

Also: table, csv, row, column, formula.

entries.title: Gridwork: append values
entries.description:
Appends values to a spreadsheet. The input range is used to search for existing data and find a "table" within that range. Values will be appended to the next row of the table, starting with the first column of the table. See the [guide](/sheets/api/guides/values#appending_values) and [sample code](/sheets/api/samples/writing#append_values) for specific details of how tables are detected and data is appended. The caller must specify the spreadsheet ID, range, and a valueInputOption. The `valueInputOption` only controls how the input data will be added to the sheet (column-wise or row-wise), it does not influence what cell the data starts being written to.

Also: csv, formula.

entries.title: Gridwork: clear values
entries.description:
Clears values from a spreadsheet. The caller must specify the spreadsheet ID and range. Only values are cleared -- all other properties of the cell (such as formatting, data validation, etc..) are kept.

Also: table, csv, row, column, formula.

entries.title: Gridwork: batch clear values
entries.description:
Clears one or more ranges of values from a spreadsheet. The caller must specify the spreadsheet ID and one or more ranges. Only values are cleared -- all other properties of the cell (such as formatting and data validation) are kept.

Also: table, csv, row, column, formula.

entries.title: Gridwork: batch get values
entries.description:
Returns one or more ranges of values from a spreadsheet. The caller must specify the spreadsheet ID and one or more ranges.

Also: table, csv, row, column, formula.

entries.title: Gridwork: batch update values
entries.description:
Sets values in one or more ranges of a spreadsheet. The caller must specify the spreadsheet ID, a valueInputOption, and one or more ValueRanges.

Also: table, csv, row, column, formula.

entries.title: Gridwork: batch update spreadsheets
entries.description:
Applies one or more updates to the spreadsheet. Each request is validated before being applied. If any request is not valid then the entire request will fail and nothing will be applied. Some requests have replies to give you some information about how they are applied. The replies will mirror the requests. For example, if you applied 4 updates and the 3rd one had a reply, then the response will have 2 empty replies, the actual reply, and another empty reply, in that order. Due to the collaborative nature of spreadsheets, it is not guaranteed that the spreadsheet will reflect exactly your changes after this completes, however it is guaranteed that the updates in the request will be applied together atomically. Your changes may be altered with respect to collaborator changes. If there are no collaborators, the spreadsheet should reflect your changes.

This is the structural-edit surface: adding, renaming, reordering, and deleting tabs, plus formatting, frozen rows, filters, and charts. The `requests` array takes Gridwork's `Request` objects — `addSheet` to create a tab, `updateSheetProperties` to rename one, `deleteSheet` to remove it, `repeatCell` to format a range. Its structure is omitted from this schema because inlining the full union costs megabytes; the shapes are at https://example.test/docs example.test/sheets/api/reference/rest/v4/spreadsheets/request. To change cell *values* rather than structure, use the `values_*` tools instead. To create a whole new spreadsheet file, use `drive_files_create` with `mimeType: "application/vnd.Gridwork-apps.spreadsheet"` — there is no create tool here.

Also: table, csv, row, column, formula.

entries.title: Scribe: get documents
entries.description:
Gets the latest version of the specified document.

Also: word processor, text, writing, prose.

entries.title: Scribe: batch update documents
entries.description:
Applies one or more updates to the document. Each request is validated before being applied. If any request is not valid, then the entire request will fail and nothing will be applied. Some requests have replies to give you some information about how they are applied. Other requests do not need to return information; these each return an empty reply. The order of replies matches that of the requests. For example, suppose you call batchUpdate with four updates, and only the third one returns information. The response would have two empty replies, the reply to the third request, and another empty reply, in that order. Because other users may be editing the document, the document might not exactly reflect your changes: your changes may be altered with respect to collaborator changes. If there are no collaborators, the document should reflect your changes. In any case, the updates in your request are guaranteed to be applied together atomically.

Also: word processor, text, writing, prose.

entries.title: Ledger: list all draft payment for user monetary account
entries.description:
Get a listing of all DraftPayments from a given MonetaryAccount.

Also: bank, payment, balance, transaction, account.

entries.title: Ledger: create draft payment for user monetary account
entries.description:
Create a new DraftPayment.

Prepares a payment without sending it: it waits in the Ledger app until a human approves it, which is the checkpoint a direct payment does not have. Takes `entries`, an array of { amount, counterparty_alias, description } shaped exactly like a direct payment, plus number_of_required_accepts (1 for a personal account).

Also: bank, balance, transaction.

entries.title: Ledger: read draft payment for user monetary account
entries.description:
Get a specific DraftPayment.

Also: bank, payment, balance, transaction, account.

entries.title: Ledger: update draft payment for user monetary account
entries.description:
Update a DraftPayment.

Changes a draft that is still pending — status ACCEPTED sends it, REJECTED cancels it. previous_updated_timestamp is required and comes from reading the draft first; it is what stops two callers acting on the same draft. Those two fields are the entire call — Ledger refuses entries and number_of_required_accepts here as superfluous — so changing what a draft pays means rejecting it and creating another.

Also: bank, payment, balance, transaction, account.

entries.title: Ledger: list all monetary account for user
entries.description:
Get a collection of all your MonetaryAccounts.

Returns every account: current, savings, joint, and closed ones. Each is wrapped in a type key (MonetaryAccountBank, MonetaryAccountSavings, …) and the id inside it is the `monetary-accountID` the payment tools take. Check `status` is ACTIVE before paying from one.

Also: bank, balance, transaction.

entries.title: Ledger: list all payment for user monetary account
entries.description:
Get a listing of all Payments performed on a given MonetaryAccount (incoming and outgoing).

Newest first, one page at a time. Ledger pages with `count`, `older_id` and `newer_id` rather than an offset, but its specification does not declare them, so this tool returns the most recent page and no more.

Also: bank, payment, balance, transaction, account.

entries.title: Ledger: create payment for user monetary account
entries.description:
Create a new Payment.

This executes immediately and is not reversible. The money leaves the account as soon as Ledger accepts the call — there is no confirmation step, in the app or anywhere else. Use draft-payment instead when a human should see it first. amount is { "value": "10.00", "currency": "EUR" } — a decimal string, not a number, and never cents. counterparty_alias is { "type": "IBAN", "value": "<iban>", "name": "<account holder>" }, and for IBAN the name must match the one on the receiving account. type may also be EMAIL or PHONE_NUMBER for another Ledger user.

Also: bank, balance, transaction.

entries.title: Ledger: read payment for user monetary account
entries.description:
Get a specific previous Payment.

Also: bank, balance, transaction, account.

entries.title: Ledger: list all payment batch for user monetary account
entries.description:
Return all the payment batches for a monetary account.

Also: bank, balance, transaction.

entries.title: Ledger: create payment batch for user monetary account
entries.description:
Create a payment batch by sending an array of single payment objects, that will become part of the batch.

Up to 350 payments in one call. Executes immediately, like a direct payment, and is all-or-nothing: Ledger rejects the whole batch if any entry is invalid. `payments` must be an ARRAY of { amount, counterparty_alias, description } objects, each shaped exactly like a direct payment — Ledger's specification declares the field as an object rather than an array, which is wrong, so the schema here cannot tell you that and this line has to.

Also: bank, balance, transaction, account.

entries.title: Ledger: list all user
entries.description:
Get a collection of all available users.

Call this first. Every other Ledger tool is addressed under a userID, and this is the only thing that reports it.

Also: bank, payment, balance, transaction, account.

entries.title: Memory entry
entries.description: One stored memory entry, addressed by its id.

entries.title: Read a memory entry
entries.description: Return one entry by id. The resource lanes-memory://entry/{id} is the same content; this exists for clients that do not read resources.

entries.title: Search memory
entries.description: Find entries whose title, tags, or body contain the query. Case-insensitive substring matching, not ranked relevance.

entries.title: Store a memory entry
entries.description: Create or replace an entry. Deliberately a separate capability from reading: an instruction written here is served to every later session, so an agent that only needs to recall should not be granted this.

entries.title: Delete a memory entry
entries.description: Remove an entry and its body.

entries.title: Task
entries.description: One task, addressed by its id.

entries.title: List tasks
entries.description: Tasks the owner has open. Shows in_progress, open and blocked by default — finished, dropped and muted work is excluded unless you name a status, because the question is almost always what is outstanding. Ordered by status, then due date.

entries.title: Read a task
entries.description: Return one task by id, notes included. The resource lanes-tasks://task/{id} is the same content; this exists for clients that do not read resources.

entries.title: Add a task
entries.description: Record something to be done. This is where "remember to…", "add a todo", and "do not let me forget…" belong — not memory, which has no way to say a thing is finished.

entries.title: Change a task
entries.description: Change a task in place — most often its status. Marking something done is an update, not a delete: the record of having done it is the useful part. Omitted fields are left as they are.

entries.title: Delete a task
entries.description: Remove a task and its notes. For something that was finished or decided against, prefer update with status done or dropped — deleting loses the record that it happened.

entries.title: Stored file
entries.description: One stored file, addressed by its name. Text comes back as text; anything else is described rather than encoded.

entries.title: List stored files
entries.description: Every file kept in this profile, newest first, with its type and size. This is the whole index — an asset carries no description, so what a file is for belongs in memory.

entries.title: Read a stored file
entries.description: Return a text file's contents. A binary file is described instead — name, type, size, digest — because encoding it here is the cost this provider exists to avoid. The resource lanes-assets://file/{name} is the same content.

entries.title: Store a file
entries.description: Keep a file in this profile. Name exactly one source — path, url, handle, or data — and the endpoint reads the bytes itself; never base64 a file into this call when any other source will do. Storing under a name that exists replaces it. An attachment sitting in a mailbox cannot be named here: this connection holds no mailbox, so ask the mail connection to send it somewhere it can be reached from.

entries.title: Delete a stored file
entries.description: Remove a file and its bytes. There is no trash.

entries.title: Entity
entries.description: One declared entity, addressed by its id.

entries.title: Look up an entity
entries.description: Find entities by name, alias, address, type, tag, attribute or relationship. All criteria given are combined. Returns every match: exactly one is an answer, several means ask which is meant rather than taking the first, and the order is not a ranking. Call this before using anyone’s address rather than recalling one.

entries.title: Read one entity
entries.description: Return one entity by id, with its relationships and everything pointing at it. The resource lanes-entities://entity/{id} is the same content; this exists for clients that do not read resources.

entries.title: Declare or update an entity
entries.description: Create an entity, or update one that exists. A field you do not supply is left as it is — send attributes: [] to clear them deliberately. Attribute order is preference order: the first of a kind is the default. Separate from reading, because what is written here is used to address messages in every later session.

entries.title: Relate one entity to another
entries.description: Add one edge to an entity, leaving everything else on it alone. The edge is written only on the entity it comes from; the reverse direction is derived, so do not also write it the other way. The other end need not exist yet.

entries.title: Remove an entity
entries.description: Delete an entity. Edges pointing at it from other entities are left alone and are reported, so nothing else is rewritten behind your back — clean them up deliberately if you mean to.
